answer:
An ETF’s quoted spread reflects the cost and risk of providing liquidity—not just trading in the ETF itself. Market makers estimate the cost of hedging with the underlying securities or related instruments. When those markets are deep and trading is cheap, hedging is generally easier; when they are thin, volatile, or closed, hedging can be costly or uncertain, so quotes may widen.

Creation and redemption also matter. If an ETF trades away from its underlying value, arbitrageurs may create or redeem shares to close the gap. Fees, operational frictions, financing, taxes, and the cost of assembling or unwinding the basket affect how readily that mechanism works and can feed into quotes.

Historical exchange volume alone is incomplete because it measures past ETF-share trading, not the liquidity or current hedging cost of the underlying basket, the availability of substitutes, or creation/redemption frictions. Quotes also respond to current volatility, market conditions, and time-zone differences. A lightly traded ETF can still have competitive quotes when its holdings are liquid; high past volume does not guarantee tight spreads in stressed or costly-to-hedge conditions.
